name: Query engines
summary: Compute that runs SQL over data it doesn’t own, and scales separately from the storage.
howItWorks: A query engine parses your SQL, asks a catalog which files hold the table, and splits the work into tasks that many workers run in parallel. Each worker reads its share of Parquet files straight from object storage, then results are shuffled, aggregated and returned through a coordinator. Because the data stays in open files, several engines can share it: an interactive SQL engine for dashboards, Spark for heavy batch and ML jobs, DuckDB on a laptop. Each one scales up, or shuts down, without moving any data.
analogy: Researchers in a public library. You can bring in one or a hundred and they all read the same shelves. When they go home, the books stay put.
useWhen: Interactive SQL over a data lake without loading it into a warehouse first
Several teams or tools that need the same tables through different engines
Spiky analytics, where paying per query or per second beats an always-on cluster
avoidWhen: Sub-second lookups for an app; use a database or a cache
Small data: DuckDB or a single Postgres is simpler than a distributed cluster
example: A retailer keeps three years of clickstream as Iceberg tables in S3. Analysts run Athena queries that each scan a few GB and pay per TB scanned. A nightly Spark job on EMR builds features from the same tables, and an engineer debugs one day’s partition with DuckDB on a laptop.

diagram.caption: Two engines share one copy of the data. Analysts’ queries go to a coordinator that hands them to a pool of workers, which grows with demand and shrinks when it’s quiet. A nightly job spins up its own Spark cluster, reads the same files and shuts down again. Neither engine owns the storage.

story: For most of database history, the SQL engine and the storage were one product: to query data, you loaded it into the database, in the database’s own format. In the late 2000s, companies such as Facebook began keeping huge datasets as plain files in Hadoop’s HDFS, because traditional warehouses had become prohibitively expensive at that size. But querying those files meant writing low-level MapReduce programs that were hard to maintain and reuse.

Facebook’s Hive, described at VLDB 2009, put SQL on top of those files. A table was just a directory, a catalog (the Hive Metastore) recorded schemas and formats, and each query compiled into MapReduce jobs; Facebook’s Hive warehouse already held over 700 TB. Hive was slow, so a wave of engines followed that read the same files without MapReduce: Google’s Dremel paper (2010) showed interactive SQL on data in place, Cloudera announced Impala and Facebook built Presto in 2012, and Spark SQL followed. AWS made the idea serverless with Athena in 2016, billing per byte scanned.

Sharing files between engines had a weakness: no transactions, so a half-finished write could corrupt a table. Table formats such as Apache Iceberg, created at Netflix in 2017, added that, which is why several engines can now safely work on the same tables.

choices.choice: A catalog that maps tables to files
choices.why: Once storage was just files, an engine needed somewhere to learn which files make up a table and how to read them. Hive’s Metastore filled that role, and later catalogs such as Glue and Iceberg REST catalogs followed the same idea.

choices.choice: Pipelined, in-memory execution instead of MapReduce
choices.why: Hive’s MapReduce jobs wrote every stage to disk. Presto and Dremel-style engines stream results between stages in memory, trading some fault tolerance for interactive speed.
Dremel’s encoding for nested columns was adopted by Apache Parquet in 2013, so any engine could read only the columns a query needs, without one vendor owning the format.
